notes:
I've put together notes on Psalm 36 from Enduring Word (Guzik), Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*, the Bible Hub and StudyLight commentary pages, Matthew Henry, and Augustine's exposition on New Advent. There are gaps:

- **NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Orthodox and catholic.com:** none of these came up.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this psalm, so there are no notes on it.
- **Protestant disagreements:** I found no clear case where one tradition reads a verse differently from another. Where commentators split (vv. 1, 6, 12), the split runs through the traditions rather than between them.

Augustine's Bible numbers this Psalm 35.

**Title / v. 1**
- **Title.** Psalm 18 is the only other psalm titled "the servant of the LORD." Trapp dates Psalm 18 to David's old age and Psalm 36 to his youth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **"Oracle."** The Hebrew word (*neum*) is normally used for God's own words, as in "says the LORD." Here it is literally "an oracle of transgression," as though David learned from watching other people's sins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Spurgeon.** He reads it the same way: people's sins speak to godly ears and show the evil inside them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/36-1.htm
- **A second reading: sin speaking inside the wicked man.** Sin is personified as the evil counsellor or prompter sitting in the heart of the wicked (Ellicott). Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and the Pulpit Commentary all note that the ancient versions and some manuscripts read "*his* heart" instead of "my heart." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/36-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed).** He takes it to mean David knows what the wicked secretly think, as if God had made him a witness to their hidden malice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-1.html
- **Barnes and Gill.** Both say it means David's own conclusion: watching how the wicked behave, he can only infer that they have no fear of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/36-1.htm
- **The root problem.** The wicked man's character rests on having no fear of God. Paul quotes this line in Romans 3:18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Augustine (Catholic/patristic).** His Latin text reads "The ungodly has said in himself that he will sin." He says the psalm describes a whole class of people who refuse to understand because they won't, not because they can't. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 2**
- **Self-flattery.** The wicked man thinks less of God and more of himself. Matthew Poole lists the ways he flatters himself: his sins aren't really sins, they are small, or good intentions excuse them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Spurgeon.** He who makes little of God makes much of himself. They who forget adoration fall into adulation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps036.cfm
- **Ellicott.** He reads verses 1 and 2 together as one pattern. On his reading, being found out may be the only thing about his sin that the wicked man hates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/36.htm
- **Augustine.** Some people look for their sin "deceitfully," afraid to find it. Once they do find it, they defend it rather than hate it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 3**
- **Pulpit Commentary.** There was a time when he sometimes acted wisely. But that time is gone by. Now he is consistently wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-36.html
- **Clarke.** His words are wicked in themselves and deceitful, meant to lead others astray. He has cut himself off from all righteousness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-36.html
- **Augustine.** The verse puts the failure in the will: "he would not understand." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 4**
- **Boice.** The wicked man isn't drifting into evil; he is inventing it. The godly use their wakeful nights to meditate on God (Psalm 1:2; 63:6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Kidner.** He notes how many of the sins listed are sins of omission: "ceased," "not good," "spurns not." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Matthew Henry.** Hardened sinners never look back on their sins with regret. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_036.cfm
- **Augustine.** "Our bed is our heart." If a person cannot be free of wickedness, let him at least hate it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 5**
- **Guzik.** The word translated "mercy" or "loving devotion" is *hesed*, God's covenant love. David can only describe it with the biggest things he knows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Spurgeon.** God's faithfulness never fails. Troubles are like clouds, but his truthfulness surrounds them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps036.cfm
- **Ellicott.** God's mercy and truth have no narrower limit than the heavens. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/36.htm
- **Augustine.** This is heavenly, eternal mercy given to the saints. The "clouds" are the preachers through whom God makes it known. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 6**
- **"Mountains of God."** This is a Hebrew way of saying "the very greatest mountains" (Pulpit Commentary). https://biblehub.com/psalms/36-6.htm
- **"The great deep."** God's judgments are unsearchable, past finding out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-6.html
- **Calvin.** If God looks after even animals, he will surely provide for people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-6.html
- **Gill (Baptist).** He allows that "righteousness" may mean God's justifying righteousness. He also mentions a figurative reading of "man and beast" as God saving Jews and Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/gnt/psalms/36-6.html
- **Biblical Illustrator.** It suggests the New Testament sense of righteousness, God's provision for saving people through Christ, also fits. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-6.html
- **Augustine.** The "mountains" are the apostles and great preachers, whom Christ lit first. The "abyss" is the depth of sin people fall into when God hands them over (Romans 1:28). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 7**
- **Kidner.** "Precious" marks the move from the immense to the intimate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **"Wings."** Some take this as the cherubim over the ark; others as a hen sheltering her chicks (Ruth 2:12; Matthew 23:37). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Coffman.** The verse shows God is the God of all people, not only Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-6.html

**v. 8**
- **Ellicott.** "Fatness" here is not sacrificial fat but grace flowing down like rain. "House" probably means heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/36.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** He applies the "fatness of God's house" to the church's worship and sacraments, with full satisfaction kept for heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_036.cfm
- **Maclaren.** The word for "delights" may echo the name "Eden." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/

**v. 9**
- **Guzik and Boice.** Boice thinks John had this verse in mind when he wrote of Christ as the true Light (John 1:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Barnes.** All life, physical and spiritual, in this world and the next, comes from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/36-9.htm
- **Clarke.** No one can light up his own soul; all understanding comes from above. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-9.html
- **Augustine.** What is the fountain of Life, but Christ? https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801036.htm

**v. 10**
- **Clarke.** Literally "draw out your mercy," keeping up the picture of a spring. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-36.html
- **Spurgeon.** God promises to keep showing mercy, yet we are still to pray for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-36/
- **Matthew Henry.** "Draw it out" as long as eternity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_036.cfm

**v. 11**
- **Calvin.** "The foot of pride" means the proud man himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-11.html
- **Keil and Delitzsch.** David pictures arrogance as a tyrant and prays not to be driven from his home into exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/36-12.htm

**v. 12**
- **Calvin and Barnes.** David speaks as if his prayer is already answered, sure that the wicked will fall. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-12.html
- **Pulpit Commentary.** The righteous may fall and get up again (Proverbs 24:16); the wicked do not. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/36-12.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist).** He reads it as a prophecy of Babylon falling to Cyrus. He reports that Augustine, Jerome and others took "there" to mean pride, the cause of all sinners' ruin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-12.html
- **Matthew Henry.** We shouldn't rejoice when a particular enemy falls, but the final defeat of all evildoers will be the saints' triumph. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/36-12.html
